To form the future perfect: avrò + participle, sarò + participle.
To use the future perfect after quando, appena, dopo che: Quando avrò finito, uscirò.
To use "entro" + future perfect: Entro marzo avremo finito.
To make guesses about the present with the simple future: Saranno le otto.
To make guesses about the past with the future perfect: Avrà perso il treno.
To use "chissà" + future: Chissà dove sarà.

Syracuse, 23rd December, half past seven in the evening. Matei, Giulia (with Viola in her pram) and Signora Concetta are waiting at the station for the train from Naples, which is bringing almost all of both families.
The train was due at six. It's already half past seven.
It must have broken down. Or there must have been a problem on the line.
It'll be stuck at Messina. In December the train ferry is always late.
My mother must have called ten times… Yes: twelve missed calls!
Graziella and Pietro must be exhausted. They left Florence at six this morning.
As soon as they've arrived, I'll give them a plate of arancini and they'll sleep like angels.
I wonder where Grandma Assunta is now. She'll have made friends with the whole carriage by now.
And my father will already have explained to the guard how to drive a locomotive.
(on the phone) Hello, Mum? … They're at Taormina! She says they'll be here in an hour.
See? Everything's fine. And when you've finished the restoration, in March, they'll all come again for the unveiling.
Let's hope so. By March we'll have finished, if all goes well.
Then by March I'll have bought another twenty lemons. With this family, there are never enough.

Careful: a-VRE-mo (we will have) ≠ a-VREM-mo (we would have). One M or two changes the meaning!
1. The future perfect: how to form it
It's formed with the auxiliary in the future (avrò / sarò) + participle. Verbs with ESSERE make the participle agree:
Don't confuse "avremo finito" (we will have finished) with "avremmo finito" (we would have finished). The double M makes the difference!
2. A future action completed before another
After quando, appena, dopo che, se, when the action will be COMPLETED before the other one, careful Italian uses the future perfect:
I'll call you after I've spoken to Bellini.
English uses the present perfect here ("when we've finished"). In spoken Italian you also hear "Quando finiamo, torniamo" — but in writing the future perfect is more correct.
"By a certain time, the action will be done": entro / per + date + future perfect.
By September Bellini will have retired.
In a year's time Viola will have learned to walk.
4. The future of probability: guesses about the present
Italian uses the simple future to make a GUESS about NOW. Romanian does exactly the same ("o fi"); English uses "must be / probably":
Dov’è Pietro? — Sarà in camera sua.
Where's Pietro? — He must be in his room.
Sure-fire trick: where English says "must be" or "I suppose", Italian often uses the future.
5. The future perfect of probability: guesses about the past
For a guess about something that HAS happened: the future perfect. In English: "must have had", "must have left".
Il treno avrà avuto un guasto.
Mia madre avrà chiamato dieci volte.
My mother must have called ten times.
He must have missed the train.
The context shows whether it's a real future or a guess: "Domani avrò finito" (tomorrow I'll have finished) / "Avrà finito, ormai" (he must have finished by now).
"Where's Pietro? — He must be in his room."

The train arrived at a quarter to nine, two hours and forty-five minutes late. Ion got off first, with the expression of a man who has just seen European civilisation collapse. "Two hours and forty-five," he said in Romanian, before even saying hello. "In forty years on the railways I've never seen anything like it." Then he saw Viola in her pram and completely forgot about the delay.

Behind him all the others got off, one after another, as if in a procession: Doina with three bags of food, Rosaria with four, Gennaro with a box of fireworks he had promised not to set off, Graziella with a panettone, Pietro with his rucksack and Signor Franco, who had decided at the last minute to come "because in Florence, without you, Christmas will be too quiet". Last of all came Grandma Assunta, helped by two young men she didn't know.

"Who can those two be?" Giulia whispered. "They'll be two students," Matei replied. "Or a couple." They were neither. They were two railway engineers from Catania, with whom Assunta and Ion had spent the whole journey discussing trains, she in Neapolitan and he in Romanian, without understanding each other in the slightest, but to the great satisfaction of both.

At Concetta's the Christmas Eve dinner had been ready for three hours. Concetta, who had cooked for fifteen, looked at the crowd coming into her little B&B and did a quick calculation. "There must be twenty," she said, "not fifteen. I must have counted wrong." Then she laid five more places without saying a word, because in Sicily, when an extra guest arrives, you set an extra place and that's that.

During dinner Doina discovered Viola's first tooth, tiny, as white as a grain of rice. The news went round the table in three languages. "It must have come through this morning," said Rosaria. "Nonsense, it must have come through from the excitement of seeing her grandparents," said Ion. Assunta wanted to touch it with one finger and pronounced: "This little girl will have a strong character. Children who cut their first tooth at Christmas are afraid of nothing." Nobody knew where this rule came from, but nobody dared contradict her.

The next day, Christmas Eve, Matei took everyone to the church to see the painting. The scaffolding was still up, but Turi had switched on all the lights. Next to the painting, on an illuminated panel, was the X-ray of the hidden child. Pietro looked at it for a long time, in silence, with his head tilted to one side. "I wonder what his name was," he said at last. "Nobody knows," Matei replied. "He must have been a child from Syracuse. He must have been about your age, more or less."

Pietro thought about it for a while. "Then I'll name him," he decided. "His name is Totò. Like Giulia's plant. That way, when the plant dies, there'll always be a Totò." Turi, who was listening from behind a column, laughed so hard he had to sit down on a pew. From that day on, all over Ortigia, the child hidden in the Caravaggio became "the Totò of Santa Lucia".

At midnight Mass the church was full. Viola, who was seven months old, was sitting up on her own for the first time, on Doina's lap, and looking at the candles with her usual seriousness. At one point she reached out towards the painting, as she had towards the wind on the ferry. Bellini, sitting in the row behind, leaned towards her. "In twenty years," he whispered, "you too will have restored a painting like this one. I won't be here any more, but I'll know anyway."

After Mass, on the terrace, among the lemon trees and the stars, the plans for the new year began. Ilinca had phoned from Sibiu: the wedding with Radu would be on the twenty-fifth of April, in the Lutheran church on the big square. "By then we'll have finished the restoration," said Giulia. "And Viola will have learned to walk," added Doina. "And I'll have learned Romanian," said Graziella, who had bought a dictionary and already knew three words: "noroc", "sarmale" and "dor".

Bellini raised his glass. "And by September," he said, "I'll have retired. So this is my last Christmas as a professor. Next year I'll just be an old gentleman who goes to look at paintings and tells everyone he used to restore them." He looked at Matei and Giulia. "And the two of you will have taken my place. God help your assistants."

Everyone laughed, but Graziella's eyes were shining with tears. "Professor," she said, "you will never be just any old gentleman. You will always be the one who brought Ernesto and Aldo back into my home." Bellini didn't answer. He just drank his wine slowly, looking at the sea.

At about two in the morning, when everyone was asleep, Gennaro climbed onto the roof with his box. He lit just one firework, a small one, which burst over the harbour in a shower of green stars. "I'd promised," he explained the next morning, when Giulia demanded an explanation. "I'd promised not to set them all off. One doesn't count." Nobody had the heart to tell him off. Especially since Viola, woken by the bang, had laughed for ten minutes.
